# MindAttic command catalog for Codex (generated by render-abilities.ps1 - MAT-T95/MAT-T98)

Codex CLI has no confirmed native "/name args" slash-command PARSER as of this writing:
`codex --help` and `codex mcp --help` list no such option, and a Codex plugin manifest
(`.codex-plugin/plugin.json`) only ever wraps `skills` (model-interpreted), `hooks`
(lifecycle events) or `mcpServers` (model-invoked tool calls) - none of the three is a
deterministic, harness-parsed command dispatch the way Claude Code's own command files are
(MAT-T98 checked `codex plugin --help`, a real bundled plugin manifest, and the plugin-creator
skill's own `plugin-json-spec.md` to confirm this - see docs/hook-contract-matrix.md).

**This catalog is the secondary, human-readable copy.** The primary, working mechanism
(CONFIRMED-WORKING, MAT-T98) is `$CODEX_HOME\skills\<name>\SKILL.md` - a plain skill folder
dropped there directly, no plugin or marketplace needed, correcting MAT-T95's assumption that
this path only holds an internal `.system` cache. A probe skill (no `.system` prefix) was
auto-discovered and invoked by a live `codex exec` run against an isolated scratch CODEX_HOME.
It is still model-interpreted from the skill's `description` (same tier as the Kimi/agy branches
below), not a true slash parser, but it costs nothing in context until matched - unlike this
catalog file, which Codex reads in full via AGENTS.md every session. Codex does read AGENTS.md
natively and does support hooks (`$CODEX_HOME\hooks.json`, wired separately under MAT-T94).
When the user types one of the names below as `/name args` or `name args` and the matching
skill folder did not already pick it up, read its entry here and follow it in plain English.
AGENTS.md should point here once (not done by this script - MAT-T95 leaves that one-line edit
for a later pass).

## /alias

Attach, replace, or clear a human nickname on a pending quicksave handoff, at any time - not just at save time. /alias <type> <real-name> <alias>.

# Alias - nickname a handoff

Global MindAttic command (MAT-T110) - works in any repo under the workspace root, with no
per-project setup. A thin wrapper for the shared runner's `alias`, which owns the registry file
and its uniqueness rules. `type` is the kind of thing being aliased; only `handoff` exists today
(covering both `/quicksave` and `/quickload`).

## 1. Find the shared runner

Walk up from the current directory until you find a folder containing
`mindattic-agent-standard\prose-agent.ps1` as an immediate child (that folder is the MindAttic
workspace root). In an orchestrator worktree (outside the workspace), use
`D:\Projects\MindAttic\mindattic-agent-standard\prose-agent.ps1`. If you can't find it, tell the
user this repo isn't under a MindAttic workspace and stop.

## 2. Parse `$ARGUMENTS`

Split on whitespace into exactly three parts: `<type> <real-name> <alias>`. If there aren't three
parts, show the usage (`/alias handoff <code> <nickname>`, e.g. `/alias handoff silky-frogs
SHADOW`) and stop without guessing. `<alias>` may itself contain spaces if the user quoted it -
pass it through as one argument either way; don't split further.

## 3. Run it

```powershell
& <workspace-root>\mindattic-agent-standard\prose-agent.ps1 alias -Type '<type>' -Code '<real-name>' -Alias '<alias>' -RepoRoot (Get-Location)
```

- **Unsupported type**: it reports only `handoff` exists today - relay that and stop.
- **No such handoff**: it reports no unconsumed handoff has that code - relay that (maybe they
  meant a different code, or it's already been consumed by a `/quickload`) and stop.
- **Alias already taken**: it names which code already holds that nickname - relay that, and
  suggest either a different nickname or aliasing the other one away first (an empty `-Alias`
  clears it: `/alias handoff <that other code> ""`).
- **Success**: it prints the confirmation, e.g. `Aliased silky-frogs as 'SHADOW'. /quickload
  SHADOW now resolves to it.` - relay that one line and stop. Do nothing else.

## Clearing a nickname

`/alias handoff <real-name> ""` (an empty third argument) removes the alias from that handoff
without touching anything else about it.

## /allocate

Auto-allocates the open tickets of this CLI's repo (or -repo=A,B, wildcards like -repo=GTFO.*, or "all") to its own subagents whenever one has a free slot, all in the repo's own checkout on main (no worktrees or branches), each landing on main and closing its ticket, until none are left. /allocate off stops it in this CLI (its subagents finish, then it quicksaves its repo's handoff); /allocate off all in every CLI; -target=PID,PID|others|all turns it on or off in other CLIs.

**Unavailable on Codex today** - Dispatches tickets to parallel subagents through Claude's Agent tool (per-ticket model selection, foreground general-purpose subagents) and reads MindAttic.Orchestrator's per-CLI gate state the same way Claude's Skill-call gating does. No portable "spawn N parallel foreground subagents with model selection" primitive is confirmed on Codex/Kimi/agy today.

**Confirmed-possible Codex equivalent (multi_agent_v2), not wired in automatically:** Codex's own spawn_agent/wait_agent/send_message/followup_task/close_agent/list_agents tool family (confirmed by MAT-T100 - a real nested mid-turn child thread, same shape as this ability's use of Claude's Agent tool) is architecturally the right primitive for the "spawn N subagents, each works a ticket" half of this ability. Not wired in as a working Codex rendering, for three honest reasons checked by MAT-T98: (1) `codex features list` shows multi_agent_v2 at stage "stable" but OFF by default (needs -c features.multi_agent_v2=true, a user-unapproved opt-in) - presenting it as drop-in parity would be dishonest; (2) whether spawn_agent exposes a per-child model-selection parameter (the way this ability picks sonnet/opus per ticket from the Orchestrator's model: line) is unconfirmed - MAT-T100's observed SubagentStart payload only showed agent_type: "default", no model field, and the app-server's generate-json-schema output has no SpawnAgent schema to check (it's a model-facing tool, not an app-server RPC); (3) Kimi/agy still have no confirmed equivalent at all, so marking this portable would be uneven across non-Claude CLIs. Treat this as a confirmed-possible path for Codex specifically, gated on the user explicitly opting into multi_agent_v2 and a follow-up confirming per-child model selection - not as something safe to silently enable today.

## /broadcast-ticket-done

After closing a ticket, tell every other live CLI (Claude, Codex, Kimi, agy - any product, any login) that it closed, so one whose own open ticket required it as a prerequisite finds out without having to poll (MAT-T105).

Run this right after `tickets ticket close <ID>`, for every ticket you close - not just
Unity.Rea.* ones. It rides entirely on infrastructure that already exists:

- MindAttic.Orchestrator's own `CliNudges` (`Sessions/CliNudges.cs`, M.ORCH-T864) already proved the
  pattern: drop a `nudge-<pid>-<kind>.txt` file in the shared session-context directory
  (`~/.claude/session-context` - a shared machine-wide location despite the name) and
  `shared/hooks/context-gate.py`'s `take_nudges()` folds it into that pid's next turn as hook
  context, never typed into its input box.
- `take_nudges()` keys purely on the CLI process's own pid (`MINDATTIC_CLI_PID` or the OS pid) - it
  has no per-product branch. Since `install-hooks.ps1` (MAT-T94) already points Claude's, Codex's,
  Kimi's and agy's hooks at this one shared `context-gate.py`, a nudge reaches whichever of those
  four products happens to own that pid, automatically - no new per-CLI code needed here.

```
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File "MindAttic.Agency\broadcast-ticket-done.ps1" `
  -TicketId <ID> -Summary "<one line: what's now true>" -ExcludePid <your own pid, if known>
```

What it does: scans every `*.state.json` under the shared session-context directory (one per CLI
turn that has ever run `context-gate.py`, any product, any login), keeps the ones whose pid still
answers (a live `Get-Process`), and leaves each a `nudge-<pid>-ticket-done.txt` reading
`Ticket <ID> closed: <Summary> Check your repo's queue (tickets ticket queue) - a prerequisite may
now be clear.`

**Named limits, not assumed away:**
- A nudge goes stale after 20 minutes if that CLI's hook never fires in that window
  (`context-gate.py`'s own `take_nudges()` constant, unmodified by this ability) - a CLI idle longer
  than that never sees it. This is a best-effort "find out sooner" layer, not the durable record:
  the ticket itself, polled with `tickets ticket show <ID> --json`, is what MAT-T103 already
  documented as the real, no-expiry, already-generic cross-CLI notification path
  (`docs/claude-only-abilities.md`, section 1c). Use both - broadcast for the CLI that happens to be
  mid-turn soon, rely on the ticket DB for the one that isn't.
- Only reaches a pid that has a `*.state.json` here already - a CLI that has never run a turn since
  being wired to the shared hooks won't show up until it does.
- This is same-machine only (the session-context directory lives under the local user profile); it
  does not reach a CLI running on a different machine.

## /bughunt

Hunt for real bugs and fix every one found. "/bughunt X" searches for X minutes then fixes everything found (the time budget bounds the search, not the fixing). "/bughunt" with no argument searches exhaustively once, then fixes everything found.

Two phases, always in this order: **search**, then **fix**. The time budget in `$ARGUMENTS`
(if any) bounds only the search phase. Once search ends, fix every bug found - no matter how
long the fix phase itself takes. The budget is never a time limit on fixing.

## 1. Parse the budget

- If `$ARGUMENTS` is a plain number, that's **X minutes** for the search phase.
- If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, there is no time budget - do one exhaustive search pass across the
  whole project instead of clock-bounding it.
- If `$ARGUMENTS` is present but not a number, ask the user to clarify rather than guessing.

## 2. Scope

Default scope is the whole current project's tracked source. Use `git ls-files` (or equivalent)
to stay inside tracked source and skip build output, dependencies, `node_modules`, `bin/`,
`obj/`, `dist/`, vendored code, lockfiles, and generated code. This is a sweep of the whole
codebase, not a review of the current diff.

## 3. Search phase - find bugs, do not fix yet

Keep a running list in your own scratch notes (not a project file) of **confirmed or
highly-plausible bugs only** - each with file:line, a one-line description, and the concrete
input/state that makes it wrong. Exclude style preferences, hypothetical hardening, and anything
that's a matter of taste rather than a real defect.

What counts as a bug: crashes, incorrect logic, null/reference errors, off-by-one errors, race
conditions and other concurrency bugs, resource/connection leaks, swallowed or mishandled
exceptions, broken error handling, security vulnerabilities (injection, auth bypass, secrets
committed in code, etc.), data loss/corruption risks, API misuse, and dead code paths that
silently produce wrong results.

Technique, in rough order:

1. Build the project (detect it from the repo: `dotnet build`, `npm run build`, `cargo build`,
   `go build ./...`, etc.). Compiler and analyzer warnings are free, high-confidence signal - start
   there. Don't run the test suite: tests run only when the user asks (GOLDEN RULE, MAT-T121).
2. Read through the source systematically, one module/service/package per pass. For independent
   areas, if your environment can run separate parallel helper agents or sub-processes (for
   example Claude Code's Agent tool, forking read-only Explore/general-purpose searches), use that
   to cover more ground within the same wall-clock budget - each fork reports findings with
   file:line back to you and fixes nothing itself. Otherwise, work through the areas sequentially.
3. Grep for bug-prone patterns relevant to the language/stack in play: unchecked nulls, `==`
   where identity/value equality is wrong, unawaited async calls, unclosed `IDisposable`/file
   handles/connections, catch blocks that swallow exceptions, string-built SQL, hardcoded
   secrets.
4. If the repo documents invariants (house rules, architecture docs, a CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md
   "Laws" section), check code against them - a violation of a documented invariant is a bug.

If a time budget was given: keep taking search passes (broadening or deepening coverage),
checking the real wall-clock elapsed time between passes (e.g. `date` or `Get-Date`) rather than
estimating. Stop the moment X minutes have elapsed, even mid-pass - whatever's been found so far
moves on to the fix phase.

If no budget was given: keep going until the whole scoped codebase has been covered once at
reasonable depth, then stop searching regardless of how long that took.

## 4. Fix phase - no time limit

Go through every recorded bug and fix it:

- Minimal, targeted fix for the actual defect - no unrelated refactors, no drive-by style
  changes, no new abstractions beyond what the fix requires.
- After each fix (or in a batch at the end, whichever is safer for the change), re-run the
  build/test suite to confirm the fix works and nothing else regressed.
- If something recorded as a "bug" turns out, on closer inspection, not to be a real defect,
  drop it and say why rather than making a no-op change.
- If something is a real bug but unsafe to auto-fix (the correct behavior is a product decision,
  or the fix is destructive/high-risk), do NOT fix it - list it separately as "needs human input"
  with the reasoning.

## 5. Report

End with a short summary: how long the search ran (or that it was unbounded), how many bugs were
found, a table of bug -> fix -> verification status, and a separate list of anything flagged but
intentionally left unfixed. Do not commit or push automatically - leave fixes in the working tree
for the user to review.

## /capture

Screenshot the app hosting this CLI (the Orchestrator tab, or the terminal when run solo) and copy the image to the clipboard.

Backed by `MindAttic.Capture`'s agent (`capture shot --self --clipboard`, M.CAPT-T77). `--self`
resolves the window to capture itself: `APP_EXE` (set by MindAttic.Orchestrator's launcher and
inherited by every tab it hosts, including through a TermHost with no window of its own) wins
first, so a CLI running as an Orchestrator tab captures the Orchestrator window; otherwise it walks
up this process's ancestors for the nearest one that owns a window - the terminal itself when the
CLI runs solo.

## 1. Find `capture.exe`

In order:
1. `capture` on PATH (only present if `MindAttic.Capture\tools\install.ps1 -AddToPath` was used).
2. `%LOCALAPPDATA%\MindAttic\Capture\bin\capture.exe` (the normal installed location).
3. Neither exists: the repo hasn't been deployed here yet. Run
   `powershell -File D:\Projects\MindAttic\MindAttic.Capture\run.ps1` once (installs `capture.exe` and
   `capture-tray.exe`), then retry step 1-2. If that repo isn't checked out either, say so and stop - don't
   build an ad hoc copy.

## 2. Capture

```
capture shot --self --clipboard
```

Image format defaults to PNG. No `--out` override: let it land in the normal `R:\MindAttic\Capture\...`
tree (or the `%USERPROFILE%\Videos\MindAttic` fallback) like every other capture.

## 3. Report

One line: the saved file path, and that it's on the clipboard, ready to paste. On failure (e.g. "No
ancestor process of this CLI owns a window to capture"), show the error as-is - don't retry with a
different target silently, since the whole point is capturing *this* CLI's own host, not a guess.

## /commit

Stage, commit, and push the current working-tree changes.

Stage, commit, and push the current working-tree changes.

Run these in parallel first:
- `git status` (no `-uall` flag - large repos)
- `git diff` (staged + unstaged)
- `git log -n 10 --oneline` (match the repo's commit-message style)

**Commit only what this session wrote.** Other agents (autopilot worktrees, other CLI tabs) may
have pending edits in the same repos, so the working tree is not "your changes". The files this
session changed are the ones its own file-edit/write actions (and its own commands) touched; go by
that, not by `git status`.
- From the **General session** (cwd is the workspace root `D:\Projects\MindAttic`, not inside a
  repo), there's no single repo: list every repo this session wrote to, and run the steps below
  once per repo with `git -C <repo>`, each with its own ticket and commit.
- Stage by explicit path (`git add -- <paths>`) only files this session changed. A file only
  someone else changed is never staged, whatever it is.
- A file this session changed that also holds someone else's uncommitted hunks: stage only your
  hunks. Write `git diff -- <file>` to a patch in the scratchpad, delete the hunks you didn't
  write, and `git apply --cached <patch>`. Check `git diff --cached -- <file>` shows only your
  work. If the hunks can't be separated cleanly, leave the file unstaged and say so.
- Afterwards, name the changes you left (other agents' files and hunks) so the user knows they
  were seen and left on purpose.

Then:
0. Log the work as a ticket with the `tickets` CLI. Every repo's tickets and stories live in the
   MindAttic.Tickets database (`MindAttic.Tickets/data/Tickets.db`). `docs/USER_STORIES.md` is a
   generated view the CLI rewrites after each change: never edit it, but stage it with the rest when it changed. Pass `--repo <name>` when you
   aren't standing in the repo (e.g. in a worktree):
   - new work: `tickets ticket new --type feature|fix|chore|docs --status closed --summary "<one line: what and why>" --ref "<story ID / test name>"`
   - work that finishes an open ticket: `tickets ticket close <CODE-Tn> --ref "<test or story>"`
     (`tickets ticket list --repo <name> --status open` shows them; `tickets ticket show <ID>` shows one with its links)
   - a story it completes: `tickets story status <CODE-US-...> done`
   Then run `tickets ticket verify` and fix anything it reports. If `tickets` isn't on PATH, stop
   and say so rather than editing any file by hand. The orchestrator commits the database itself.
   **One ticket per commit, no cross-contamination.** If this session's changes cover more than
   one ticket or story, make one commit per ticket: repeat steps 0-6 for each, staging only that
   ticket's files and hunks. Never fold another ticket's work, or unticketed work, into a commit.
1. Draft a concise (1-2 sentence) commit message focused on the *why*, not the *what*. Match the
   recent log's tone. The subject line MUST end with the ticket ID in parentheses, e.g.
   `... (M.ORCH-T56)`, and the ID must exist in the ticket database: every repo's `commit-msg`
   hook refuses anything else. No ticket ID, no commit: go back to step 0 and create the ticket.
2. Stage this session's files by name (see above). Never `git add -A`, `git add .` or `git commit -a`: they pull in other agents' work as well as `.env` files, credentials and large binaries.
3. Skip secrets: warn before committing anything that looks like a credential file.
4. Create a NEW commit (never `--amend`), ending with the attribution footer this session was
   given - the `Co-Authored-By:` line, plus a session-reference line whenever one is provided.
   Do NOT hardcode a model name here: it goes stale the moment the model changes, and a commit
   log that credits the wrong model is worse than one that credits none. If the session was given
   no attribution guidance, omit the footer rather than guessing.
   Pass the message via heredoc so multi-line formatting is preserved.
5. Run `git status` after the commit and confirm it succeeded.
6. Push to the upstream remote (`git push`). If the branch has no upstream yet, push with `-u origin <branch>`. Surface the remote's response - and if the push is rejected (e.g. non-fast-forward), STOP and report to the user instead of force-pushing.
   Before pushing, note the range being pushed (`git rev-parse @{u}` .. `HEAD`); step 6b needs it.
6b. **Push git subtrees too.** A repo can embed another repo as a `git subtree` (e.g. a `shared/`
   folder). Its changes only reach that other repo through `git subtree push`, so `/commit` does it
   every time; it is part of committing, not a separate cross-repo action, so no `/crossrepo` is needed.
   - Find the subtrees: the `git-subtree-dir: <prefix>` lines in `git log --grep=git-subtree-dir: --format=%B`,
     unique. None: skip this step. History keeps a folder that was folded in for good, so skip any prefix
     the repo's `AGENTS.md` says is no longer a subtree.
   - For each prefix, check whether the pushed range touched it: `git log --oneline <old upstream>..HEAD -- <prefix>`.
     Nothing: skip that prefix.
   - Find its upstream: the URL and branch the repo's `AGENTS.md` (or README) gives for that subtree,
     else a remote named after it. Can't find one: don't guess; say which prefix has unpushed changes.
   - Run `git subtree push --prefix <prefix> <url> <branch>` (it can take minutes on long histories)
     and surface the output. If it is rejected because the upstream moved on, STOP and report: the
     fix is `git subtree pull --prefix <prefix> <url> <branch> --squash`, then `/commit` again. Never
     force-push a subtree upstream, and never push to a remote the repo's `AGENTS.md` forbids.
7. Print the commit hash + a one-line summary, and each subtree pushed (prefix -> upstream).

Do NOT skip hooks (`--no-verify`). Do NOT force-push. If a pre-commit hook fails, fix the underlying issue and create a fresh commit - never amend. If a push to `main`/`master` is rejected, warn the user before any recovery action; do not force-push protected branches.

If there are no changes, say so and exit without creating an empty commit (and skip the push).

## /crossrepo

Let this CLI work other repos too (the one exception to "a repo's window works only that repo"). /crossrepo off ends it.

/crossrepo $ARGUMENTS is running in this CLI. MindAttic.Orchestrator's gates record it for this CLI
process, until it closes, when the user typed it, or when you invoked it yourself as a direct
response to the user's own latest request for cross-repo work (for example, a command/skill
mechanism the user's own prompt asked for); an invocation the user didn't ask for is refused and
records nothing, so never start it on your own.

If the arguments are empty or "off": reply with one short line confirming this window is back to its own repo only.

Otherwise reply with one short line confirming this window may now also edit and close tickets in the repos named ("all" means any repo), then carry on with whatever was asked.

## /deploy

Deploy the current project using whatever deploy mechanism it actually has.

Global MindAttic command. There is no single deploy mechanism across the workspace - this command
is a router, not a shared implementation: it figures out which mechanism *this* repo actually uses
and defers to it. Never invent deploy steps that aren't backed by one of the cases below.

## 1. A project-owned `run.ps1`

If the current repo root (or its `tools/` folder) has a `run.ps1`, that is authoritative (it was
named `deploy.ps1` before 2026-10-27; treat an old `deploy.ps1` the same way). Run it
non-interactively with PowerShell (passing `$ARGUMENTS` through as its own flags) and report its
output. Never run the generated `run.bat` launcher: it opens a Deploy & Run / Run menu and waits for
a keypress. Do not second-guess what the script does.

## 2. Routed through MindAttic.Deploy

Else, look for `..\MindAttic.Deploy\projects.json` (walk up to the workspace root first, same as
`/quicksave`, if `..` isn't it directly). If this repo's name appears in its `projects[]`, `sites[]`
or `apps[]` arrays, deploy through MindAttic.Deploy's own CLI/npm entry point for that entry - read
MindAttic.Deploy's README for the current invocation (e.g. `npm run deploy -- --only <slug>`)
rather than guessing the flag shape, and report its output.

## 3. Neither applies

Tell the user plainly that this repo has no automated deploy configured - name what you checked
(no `run.ps1`, not listed in MindAttic.Deploy's `projects.json`) - and stop. Do not fabricate a
deploy path. If the repo's own `AGENTS.md`/`README.md` documents a manual publish step (e.g. "edit
README.md and push to main" for a README-as-product repo), relay that instead of just saying no.

## Always

- Never force-push, skip hooks, or bypass a failing build to "just get it deployed."
- Surface whatever the underlying script/CLI prints - don't summarize away a failure.
- If credentials are missing (FTP, Azure, NuGet feed), say which ones rather than retrying blindly.

## /do

Continue the current task without re-asking for confirmation or clarification.

Continue the current task without re-asking for confirmation or clarification.

This is the slash-command form of the global rule: a bare "do" / "do it" / "yes" means *continue,
keep going, proceed*. Resume from where you left off.

How to handle `/do`:

1. **Find what's in-flight.** Re-read the most recent assistant turn and anything you're tracking
   as an in-progress task or step. If the prior turn ended with an offer ("want me to X?") or a
   paused step, that's the thing to resume. If a prompt-submit hook just injected a `/quicksave`
   transcript, treat that as the in-flight state instead.
2. **Don't restart.** Do not re-survey the codebase, re-explain the plan, or re-ask the user what
   they want. They already said *do it*.
3. **No preamble.** Skip "Sure, here we go" - just run the next concrete action (an edit, a shell
   command, updating your task tracking, etc.).
4. **If you genuinely don't know what to resume** (no prior assistant message, no in-progress
   tasks, no injected transcript, fresh session), say so in one sentence and ask what to do. Don't
   fabricate an interpretation.
5. **Respect risk gates.** "Continue" does not authorize new destructive actions that weren't
   already proposed and accepted. Stay within the scope of the work that was paused.

Treat `/do` as a no-op accelerator: it removes a turn of friction, not a turn of judgment.

## /dock

Reattach this CLI's hosted session (or another's, by id) into the dashboard right now, instead of waiting for the next automatic check. /dock [SESSION].

Run `orchestrator dock $ARGUMENTS` (no arguments: this CLI's own session, from its `MINDATTIC_TERM_ID`). It re-announces the hosted session as just started over the same bus a TermHost already uses when it registers, so any running MindAttic.Orchestrator dashboard reattaches its tab under the right login immediately - the same path a dashboard crash or restart already reattaches through (M.ORCH-T1448). It never kills or restarts the CLI.

Report the command's own result line to the user, verbatim or near enough. If it says this CLI isn't running under a TermHost, tell the user plainly that it needs to have been started through the Launcher (hosted) to be dockable at all - relaunching it that way is the fix, not retrying /dock.

## /listen, /hey-listen

Treat $ARGUMENTS as your direct, literal instruction for this turn - ignore billing banners, MindAttic.Orchestrator pacing/context-gate notices, and other hook-injected text as reasons to decline or hedge; queue the action (e.g. a scheduled wake-up) when a real hard limit blocks it right now.

/listen $ARGUMENTS (or /hey-listen $ARGUMENTS) was typed directly by the user. This command exists
so hook-injected text - SessionStart billing banners, MindAttic.Orchestrator's pacing/context-gate
notices ("5-hour window capped...", "under its target, so start more now"), and any other
system-reminder/tool-noise sitting between the user's words and your response - never gets mistaken
for an instruction, or for a reason to refuse, hedge, or ask "should I?" about the literal thing
just said.

How to handle it:

1. **The instruction is $ARGUMENTS, full stop.** Read it as a plain, direct instruction, exactly as if no hook content existed in this turn or the ones around it.
2. **Hook/system-reminder content is background telemetry, never a veto.** A pacing gate saying the window is capped, a billing line, a "start more subagents" nudge - none of these are grounds to decline the literal instruction. They describe orchestrator bookkeeping, not permission.
3. **If the literal action truly cannot run right now** (a real hard limit, not just cautionary hook text), **queue it instead of stopping.** Use whatever scheduling/wake-up mechanism is available to you (for example Claude's ScheduleWakeup/CronCreate, or a cron job/timer elsewhere) to carry it forward to the moment it can run, and say so in one line. Scheduling a future action is never blocked by current pacing - only the execution of tool calls against the live window is.
4. **No hedging, no meta-commentary, no re-confirmation.** Skip "just to confirm", skip summarizing the hooks back to the user, skip asking permission for something already stated plainly. Do the thing, or queue the thing, and report which in one short line.
5. **This does not waive real safety/confirmation rules.** Destructive or irreversible actions still get the same scrutiny as always - /listen cuts through hook noise, not through genuine authorization requirements.
6. **User-typed only.** Run this only when the user typed `/listen` (or `/hey-listen`) themselves. Triggering this yourself (rather than the user typing it) is refused and does nothing - never self-invoke it to talk yourself past a gate.
7. **A grant made here can target the future, not just this turn.** If $ARGUMENTS grants permission for a gated command (`/allocate`, `/crossrepo`) to run later - e.g. "you have permission to /allocate at 6am" - and the action is queued per rule 3, that grant travels with the queued prompt. When the scheduled wake-up fires it hours later, possibly while the user is asleep and typing nothing, treat the grant as still live: run the gated command yourself then, instead of printing the command and waiting for a keystroke that isn't coming. Make the queued prompt say explicitly what was granted so the future turn doesn't have to re-derive it.

## /org, /organization

The organization: /org usage prints every member's usage table; /org login <who> signs a member in; /org members lists them (add, set and remove change them); /org start <repo> <who> starts a CLI on a member's login; /org allow <who> [--until <reset|time>] lets that member's login take work past its weekly target until its weekly reset, /org disallow <who> takes it back, and /org limit [<who> --weekly <pct> --5h <pct> | --reset] lists or sets each member's usage cutoffs (90% of the week and 96% of the 5-hour window by default). <who> is a member's email, the part before the @, name, first name, login alias or initials. Each works on the org chosen in the dashboard's switcher; --org <id|name> picks another. /org help lists them.

/org $ARGUMENTS (or /organization $ARGUMENTS) was asked for. All it does is run
MindAttic.Orchestrator's CLI: do nothing else, and don't work out any answer yourself.

If the arguments start with "login": that opens a browser sign-in, which has to run in the user's own terminal, so don't run it. Reply with only this line, for the user to type at the prompt:
`! orchestrator org $ARGUMENTS`

If the arguments start with "allow" or "disallow", or are "limit" with a member and a percent or --reset: letting a login past its weekly target or changing its cutoffs is the user's decision alone, so run it only when the user's own latest prompt asked for it, never on your own, for another agent, or to get a ticket worked.

Otherwise (allow, disallow and limit changes included, once the user asked) run `orchestrator org $ARGUMENTS` (from any folder) and show what it prints exactly as printed, in one code block so the table's columns line up: no summary, nothing reformatted, left out or added. Then end your turn.

## /pacing

/pacing off runs this CLI without pace holds until it closes or /pacing on (the default for every new CLI); a bare /pacing says which this CLI is on. The 99% and weekly stops still apply.

/pacing $ARGUMENTS was typed in this CLI, and MindAttic.Orchestrator's context gate has recorded it
for this CLI process only. With off: no pace holds (subagents included) until the CLI closes or
/pacing on is typed; its usage still counts toward the 5-hour pace, so other CLIs absorb it, and the
stop at the window's target and the weekly stop still apply. With on: this CLI is held to the pace
again. Reply with one short line confirming which, then carry on with whatever was asked.

## /progress

Show what every running subagent is doing and roughly what percent done each one is.

Show subagent progress. The shared runner does the work; this ability only invokes it.

1. Run, passing through any arguments the user gave (`$ARGUMENTS`):

   ```powershell
   powershell -NoProfile -File D:\Projects\MindAttic\mindattic-agent-standard\agent-progress.ps1 $ARGUMENTS
   ```

2. Show its report to the user as-is, in a code block so the bars line up. It covers every
   session and project, so subagents of other CLIs appear too (their session id and project are

3. Under it, add at most three short lines of your own:
   - anything marked `stalled?` (no activity for 10+ minutes while not finished): name it and

   - for this CLI's own subagents, anything you know that the transcript can't show (for

The percent is an estimate. A ticket agent is placed by the milestones it has reached:

tool calls only and shown with a `~`. Say "about" when you quote a percent.

Inside the Prose repo, Prose's own project `/progress` (its strand dashboard) takes precedence; this
command is everywhere else.

## /publish

Build the current repo's mod, skip the whole thing if nothing actually changed, otherwise bump its version, write a player-facing changelog and README update, and publish to NexusMods and/or Thunderstore (whichever the repo is configured for) via a GitHub release that triggers CI by default.

Global MindAttic command for a repo that ships a mod. Supports two independent platforms, each
gated on its own config file - a repo may have one or the other:

- **NexusMods** - `nexus.json` at the repo root:
  ```json
  { "modId": 651, "fileId": 12345, "modFolderName": "RogueTraderBrevity", "project": "src/BrevityMod", "category": "main" }
  ```
- **Thunderstore** - `thunderstore.toml` at the repo root (GTFO mods). Name/namespace/version come
  from `package/manifest.json`, which `thunderstore.toml` itself says is the source of truth for
  `tcli publish --file <zip>`.

If neither config file exists, tell the user plainly this repo has no automated publish configured,
and stop - never fabricate IDs. For NexusMods, if `fileId` is `0` or absent, stop and say which
field still needs filling in (get it from the mod page's Files tab -> API Info, or Manage Files ->
edit menu).

## 1. Build the current (unbumped) version

- RogueTrader mods: `dotnet build <nexus.json's project> -c Release` (per
  `RogueTrader.Package.targets`, this packages into `<project>\obj\Release\<tfm>\package\<ModFolderName>\`
  before zipping to `dist\<modFolderName>-<version>.zip` - glob for the `<tfm>` segment, it varies
  per project). The pre-zip folder `.../package/<ModFolderName>/` is the payload to hash.
- GTFO mods: `./build.ps1` from the repo root. `package/` (repo root, not `dist/`) is the payload to
  hash - it's rebuilt in place from `src/` output each run, same folder Thunderstore ships.

## 2. No-op guard - never bump or republish unmodified code

Read `.publish-state.json` at the repo root (`{ "lastPublishedVersion": "...", "lastPublishedHash":
"...", "lastPublishedRef": "<git sha>" }`). If it doesn't exist, this is the first tracked publish -
skip the comparison below but still create the file after a successful publish.

Hash the payload directory from step 1 with
`mindattic-agent-standard/shared/compute-mod-hash.ps1 -Path <payload dir> -ExcludeNames <...>`.
**Exclude every file whose content is expected to change on every publish regardless of whether the
compiled/packaged mod itself changed** - otherwise the hash can never repeat and the guard is
useless:
- RogueTrader: the mod's own manifest (`Info.json` for Brevity, `OwlcatModificationManifest.json`
  for Overwatch) embeds the version string.
- GTFO: `manifest.json`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `README.md`.

This hashes actual payload bytes, not the zip - zip format embeds timestamps and can
reorder/recompress identical content differently between builds, which would make an unchanged mod
look "changed". Don't substitute a zip-file hash or a git-diff-since-last-tag check for this.

**If the new hash equals `lastPublishedHash`:** tell the user plainly, e.g. "No code changes since
v<lastPublishedVersion> - skipping publish (payload hash unchanged)," and stop. Do not touch the
version, changelog, README, or cut a release. This is the point of the whole guard.

**If it differs (or there's no prior state):** continue to step 3.

## 3. Bump the version

Read the current version from its canonical source (RogueTrader: the `Info.json`/
`OwlcatModificationManifest.json` field the `.csproj`'s `ModVersion` regex reads; GTFO:
`package/manifest.json`'s `version_number`, keep `thunderstore.toml`'s `versionNumber` in sync).
Increment the leading integer by 1, preserving whatever suffix format was already there (a bare
integer stays bare; an `X.0.0` triple stays `X.0.0` - Thunderstore requires strict semver, this repo
family only ever bumps the major component). Write the new version back, then rebuild (step 1's
command again) so the dist zip/package reflects it.

If a GTFO mod's `AGENTS.md` documents a cross-repo dependency pin on another MindAttic mod's version
(e.g. GTFO.EZ's `MindAttic-GtfoEZAbsurdItems-X.Y.Z` in `package/manifest.json`), check whether that
pinned mod also needs a bump per that doc's own rule before assuming it's unrelated - don't silently
leave a stale pin.

## 4. Write a player-facing changelog entry

`git log <lastPublishedRef>..HEAD --oneline` lists every commit since the last publish (each ends
with its ticket ID, per house convention). Read any whose summary alone doesn't make the user-facing
effect clear (`git show <sha>`), then write 2-6 genuine, player-facing bullets - what changed for
someone playing the mod, not ticket titles or raw commit text - grouped as Added/Changed/Fixed only
when that helps; a small release can stay a flat list. Match the repo's own existing changelog voice
(GTFO.EZ's `package/CHANGELOG.md` bolds a short headline per entry, explains the player-visible
effect in plain language, then cites the ticket ID in parentheses - follow that pattern). Cite each
entry's ticket ID the same way.

Prepend the new `## <version>` entry to:
- GTFO: `package/CHANGELOG.md` (existing convention, ships in the Thunderstore package and renders
  on its listing page).
- RogueTrader (no existing CHANGELOG.md): a `## Changelog` section in the repo's `README.md`,
  newest version first; create the section if it doesn't exist yet.

## 5. Review the README(s) for accuracy

Bump every version reference. Then **read the whole README end to end** (repo root, and GTFO's
`package/README.md` which ships in the Thunderstore package) and compare its prose against the
actual current code/behavior - not just the commits since last publish, the whole document. Correct
anything stale: a described feature that no longer works that way, a removed option still
documented, a stated limitation that's since been fixed, wrong file paths. This is a judgment pass,
not a mechanical one - read the source for anything you're not sure is still accurate rather than
assuming the README was already correct.

## 6. Record the publish state and commit

Write `.publish-state.json` with the new hash (recompute after the step-3 rebuild, in case the
version bump itself changed payload bytes - e.g. an embedded version string in a DLL), the new
version, and `lastPublishedRef` set to the commit you're about to make (fill in its real sha after
committing). Commit the version-bump file(s), changelog, README(s) and `.publish-state.json` together
under one ticket, by path (never a bare `git commit`), and push.

**This commit happens before the upload is confirmed.** If the CI run in step 7 (or the local
fallback) fails, the state file already claims this version as published - don't leave that
standing: tell the user plainly that the version/changelog/README landed but the upload itself
failed, and that retrying needs the upload step re-run directly (`gh workflow run publish.yml` or
the local fallback script), not a second `/publish` - a second `/publish` will see the hash already
matches and skip.

## 7. Cut the release (triggers CI) - the default path

Unless `--local` was passed:

- `git tag v<version>` and `git push origin v<version>`.
- `gh release create v<version> "dist\<modFolderName>-<version>.zip"` (RogueTrader) or
  `"dist\<DisplayName>-<version>.zip"` (GTFO, per `build.ps1`) `--title "<name> <version>" --notes
  "<the changelog entry from step 4>"`. Attaching the zip as a release asset is what lets CI publish
  it without needing the game (or, for GTFO, a configured BepInEx profile) on the runner.
- That `release: published` event is what the repo's `.github/workflows/publish.yml` listens for: it
  downloads the release asset and runs `Nexus-Mods/upload-action` (NexusMods repos, using
  `NEXUSMODS_API_KEY`) and/or installs `tcli` and runs `tcli publish --file <zip> --token
  $env:THUNDERSTORE_API_KEY` (Thunderstore repos). Watch it with `gh run list --workflow publish.yml
  -L 1` then `gh run watch <run-id>`, and report its real outcome - don't claim success before it
  finishes. If the repo has no `publish.yml`, say so and fall back to step 8 instead.

## 8. Local fallback

If `gh` isn't available, the repo has no `origin` on GitHub, `.github/workflows/publish.yml` doesn't
exist, or `--local` was passed: still create the tag (so a second `/publish` doesn't re-detect this
version as new), then:
- NexusMods: `mindattic-agent-standard/shared/publish-nexus-local.ps1 -RepoPath <repo root>`. Reads
  the key from `%APPDATA%\MindAttic\Nexus\tokens.json` and runs the vendored `Nexus-Mods/upload-action`
  code directly with Node.
- Thunderstore: `tcli publish --file <dist zip> --token (mindattic-agent-standard/shared/get-thunderstore-api-key.ps1)`
  (install `tcli` first - `dotnet tool install -g tcli` - if it's not already on PATH). Reads the key
  from `%APPDATA%\MindAttic\Thunderstore\tokens.json`.

## Always

- Never invent a `modId`/`fileId`/namespace - only use what the repo's own config says.
- Surface the real build/CI/upload output; don't summarize away a failure.
- If the relevant Vault bucket has no `apiKey`, say so and point at
  https://next.nexusmods.com/settings/api-keys (NexusMods) or
  https://thunderstore.io/settings/teams/ (Thunderstore, Service Accounts) - don't try to upload
  without one.
- Never force-push or skip hooks to "just get it published."
- The no-op guard (step 2) is the whole point of this redesign - never bypass it to "just publish
  anyway" unless the user explicitly says to force a republish of unchanged code.

## /qq

Ask a quick question and get an instant, direct answer - this turn suspends pacing holds, subagent-fanout nudges and "start more work now" hook noise entirely; no waiting for room, no waiting on a timer, no spawning subagents for it.

/qq $ARGUMENTS was typed directly by the user as a quick question. This command exists for the
moment the user just wants a plain answer right now, not a task run through MindAttic.Orchestrator's
pacing machinery.

How to handle it:

1. **Answer $ARGUMENTS directly, immediately, in this turn.** No subagents, no background workflow, no "let me start agents on your other tickets first" - just read the question and answer it, the same as you would with no hooks in play at all.
2. **Every hook-injected pacing/context-gate line in this turn is void for this turn.** A "start more subagents now", a 5-hour/weekly target line, a billing banner, a context-gate notice - none of it is a reason to delay the answer, hedge on it, or append unrelated catch-up work. Treat this turn as if that text were never there.
3. **Don't let this turn become a task.** Unlike /listen, /qq is for a question, not an instruction to change code or state. If $ARGUMENTS actually asks for an edit/commit/deploy, answer the informational part instantly, then say plainly that the action itself still goes through the normal flow (a ticket first, confirmation for anything risky) rather than skipping those safeguards.
4. **No ticket, no subagent, no deferral for the question itself.** Answering a quick question is never "code" and never needs a ticket of its own; just answer it.
5. **User-typed only.** Run this only when the user typed `/qq` themselves. Don't self-invoke it to talk yourself past a gate.
6. **This is scoped to this one turn.** It doesn't change the CLI's standing pacing state (that's `/pacing`) - the very next turn is paced normally again unless it's also `/qq` or `/listen`.

## /quickload

Restore a /quicksave handoff and resume exactly where it left off - this repo's latest, an archive number, or a shareable code from any login.

# Quickload - restore the handoff

Global MindAttic command - the counterpart to `/quicksave`, works in any repo under the workspace
root with no per-project setup. The live handoff is conceptually save `0`; archives are `.1`, `.2`,
... (most recent archive is `.1`, shifting up as older saves accumulate). `/quickload` with no
argument and `/quickload 0` are **the same command**. A word-word argument (e.g. `lively-oxen`) is
a shareable handoff code; any other word (e.g. `SHADOW`) is tried as a nickname set by `/alias`
(MAT-T110) - the runner resolves either one the same way, so just pass through whatever the user
typed.

## 0. Find the shared runner

Walk up from the current directory until you find a folder containing
`mindattic-agent-standard\prose-agent.ps1` as an immediate child (that's the MindAttic workspace
root). In an orchestrator worktree (outside the workspace), use
`D:\Projects\MindAttic\mindattic-agent-standard\prose-agent.ps1`. If you can't find it, tell the
user this repo isn't under a MindAttic workspace and stop.

## A handoff code or nickname - `/quickload <code>` (e.g. `/quickload lively-oxen` or `/quickload SHADOW`)

Loads that exact handoff from the machine-wide registry, whichever login and folder saved it - a
literal code and a nickname set by `/alias` both work here, tried in that order:

```powershell
& <workspace-root>\mindattic-agent-standard\prose-agent.ps1 load <code-or-nickname> -RepoRoot (Get-Location)
```

- If it reports neither a code nor a nickname matched: tell the user, and stop. (`/quicksaves` lists
  every pending one with its code and nickname, if they want to pick one.)
- Otherwise it prints Code / Repo (with worktree and branch) / Saved by / Task / Decisions /
  State / Next / Universe / Updated and any queued bookmarks, and consumes the code (archived to
  the registry's `consumed\` folder, never deleted; the code is free for reuse). A code that was
  already consumed is recalled read-only, with a note saying so.
  1. Briefly confirm what you're resuming (one line), including the code.
  2. If the **Repo** path is not the current folder, the work lives there: say so, and work in
     that repo/worktree (subject to the usual one-repo-per-window rules).
  3. Pick up the **Task**, honor every **Decision**, and continue from **Next** without
     re-asking anything already settled.

## No argument, or `0` - `/quickload` / `/quickload 0`

Run, from the current repo root:

```powershell
& <workspace-root>\mindattic-agent-standard\prose-agent.ps1 load -RepoRoot (Get-Location)
```

- If it reports no handoff exists: tell the user there's nothing to restore, and stop.
- Otherwise it prints the same fields, and - as a side effect - archives the live handoff to
  `.agent\agent-session.json.001` (older archives shift up) and consumes its shareable code.
  That's expected: it is consumed for resume purposes only, never lost.
  1. Briefly confirm to the user what you're resuming (one line).
  2. Pick up the **Task**, honor every **Decision**, and continue from **Next** without
     re-asking anything already settled.

## A positive number - `/quickload <N>` (e.g. `/quickload 1`, `/quickload 3`)

The runner has no subcommand for this - recall one specific archive directly and read-only,
**without consuming or rotating anything**:

1. Read `.agent\agent-session.json.NNN` in the current repo root, zero-padded to 3 digits
   (`.001`, `.002`, ...).
2. If that exact archive doesn't exist: tell the user, list the archive numbers that *do* exist
   (`.agent\agent-session.json.*` in the repo root), and stop. Don't guess which one they meant.
3. If it exists: treat its `task` / `decisions` / `state` / `next` fields as your authoritative
   working memory for this session, same as the no-argument case - but leave every file on disk
   exactly as it is. This is a read-only recall ("what was I doing two saves ago"), not a
   consume-and-resume.
   - Briefly confirm which archive you loaded (e.g. "Resuming from agent-session.json.003: ...").
   - Pick up its **Task**, honor its **Decisions**, and continue from its **Next** without
     re-asking anything already settled. If the live handoff or a more recent archive describes a
     *different* task, say so - the user asked for this specific one on purpose, but a stale plan
     is worth flagging.

## /quicksave

Save the current discussion as a handoff so it survives /clear; restore with a bare 'do', /quickload, or /quickload <code> from any login's CLI.

# Quicksave

Global MindAttic command - works in any repo under the workspace root, with no per-project setup.
It's a thin alias for the shared runner's `save`: the runner owns the handoff file and its
archiving (never overwritten, never deleted - an unconsumed prior save is shifted to
`.agent\agent-session.json.001`, older ones shifting up). This alias only fills in what to save.

Every save also gets a short shareable code (adjective-animal, e.g. `lively-oxen`) and is recorded
in the machine-wide handoff registry (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\MindAttic\handoffs`, shared by every login),
with the repo/worktree it was made in. `/quickload <code>` loads that exact handoff from any
login's CLI, in any folder.

## 1. Find the shared runner

Walk up from the current directory until you find a folder containing
`mindattic-agent-standard\prose-agent.ps1` as an immediate child (that folder is the MindAttic
workspace root; the current repo is one of its direct subfolders). In an orchestrator worktree
(outside the workspace), use `D:\Projects\MindAttic\mindattic-agent-standard\prose-agent.ps1`.
If you can't find it, tell the user this repo isn't under a MindAttic workspace and stop - don't
guess a path.

## 2. Compose the handoff

Write four fields about the *current* discussion - what a fresh session needs to resume without
re-asking anything. Be concrete: file paths, names, ids, exact commands. If `$ARGUMENTS` is
non-empty, it's a nickname (e.g. `SHADOW`) - lead **Task** with it too, for readability, but the
nickname itself is set as a real alias in step 4, not just embedded in the text.

- **Task** - the one thing we are mid-work on, as a resumable instruction.
- **Decisions** - what is settled and must not be re-litigated.
- **State** - what's done, what's in flight, the last action and its result.
- **Next** - the next concrete steps, numbered, the very next action first.

## 3. Save it

Run it from the current repo root with PowerShell (single-quote the strings, doubling any `'`
inside them):

```powershell
& <workspace-root>\mindattic-agent-standard\prose-agent.ps1 save -RepoRoot (Get-Location) `
  -Task '<task>' -Decisions '<decisions>' -State '<state>' -Next '<next>'
```

It prints the handoff code it picked.

## 4. Alias it, if `$ARGUMENTS` was non-empty (MAT-T110)

```powershell
& <workspace-root>\mindattic-agent-standard\prose-agent.ps1 alias -Type handoff -Code '<the printed code>' -Alias '<the nickname from $ARGUMENTS>' -RepoRoot (Get-Location)
```

If it reports the nickname is already taken by a different code, tell the user that plainly
(naming the other code) rather than silently skipping the alias - the save itself already
succeeded either way. Skip this step entirely when `$ARGUMENTS` was empty.

## 5. Confirm

Tell the user in one line that it's saved and give the code (and nickname, if one was set): run
`/clear`, then type `do` (or `/quickload`) here, or `/quickload <code or nickname>` from any
login's CLI. Do nothing else.

## /quicksaves

A brochure of every pending quicksave handoff - code, alias, repo, and a short description of what it's about - so you can find the one to resume.

# Quicksaves - browse pending handoffs

Global MindAttic command (MAT-T109, renamed from `/handoffs` in MAT-T113 - a handoff *is* what
`/quicksave` creates, so this list is named after the command family it sits beside) - works in
any repo under the workspace root, with no per-project setup. Lists every **unconsumed** handoff
in the machine-wide registry (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\MindAttic\handoffs`, shared by every login) - a
handoff already restored by `/quickload` is consumed and won't appear. Give one nickname with
`/alias` (see that command) if a handoff doesn't have one and should.

## 1. Find the shared runner

Walk up from the current directory until you find a folder containing
`mindattic-agent-standard\prose-agent.ps1` as an immediate child (that folder is the MindAttic
workspace root). In an orchestrator worktree (outside the workspace), use
`D:\Projects\MindAttic\mindattic-agent-standard\prose-agent.ps1`. If you can't find it, tell the
user this repo isn't under a MindAttic workspace and stop.

## 2. Fetch the data

```powershell
& <workspace-root>\mindattic-agent-standard\prose-agent.ps1 quicksaves -Json
```

This returns every unconsumed handoff, newest first, as JSON objects with at least `code`,
`repo.name`, `updatedAt`, `task`. Two fields matter most for this brochure when present:

- **`alias`** - a human nickname set by `/alias` (e.g. `SHADOW`, `REMOTE`). Most handoffs won't
  have one.
- **`description`** - a ready-made summary, 255 characters or fewer, of what the handoff is
  about. Use it verbatim when present - don't re-summarize it.

If a handoff has no `description` field (an older save, from before this field existed), write
one yourself from its `task`/`state`/`decisions` fields: plain English, 255 characters or fewer,
no mid-sentence truncation - end on a full clause.

## 3. Render it as a brochure, not a table

A straight table doesn't fit a 255-character description in a column. Instead, print one block
per handoff, newest first:

```
━━━ SHADOW · silky-frogs ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Repo:      MindAttic
Updated:   2026-11-06 20:37
Researched hosting the Orchestrator with a real GPU so agents could run/
playtest Unity, Unreal and s&box games. Shadow PC rejected as too specialized/
costly; superseded by REMOTE, a RAM-only host with no GPU need.
```

- The heading line is the alias (if any) and the code, e.g. `SHADOW · silky-frogs`; a handoff
  with no alias just shows its code alone, e.g. `early-badgers`.
- `Updated` in local time, human-readable (`yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm` is fine).
- Wrap the description to a comfortable terminal width (about 78 columns); don't print it as one
  unbroken line.
- A blank line between blocks.
- If there are none: say plainly there are no pending handoffs right now.

## 4. Close with how to use one

One short line after the brochure: `/quickload <code or alias>` restores any of these from any
login's CLI (e.g. `/quickload SHADOW` or `/quickload silky-frogs`); `/alias handoff <code>
<name>` gives an unnamed one a nickname.

## /research

Hand a research question to another org member's login - /research <who> <what> starts a CLI on their login in this repo that answers it, saves the answer to docs/research/, commits it and messages you back.

**Unavailable on Codex today** - MAT-T103 traced this to two separate, confirmed reasons, not just SendMessage (full detail in docs/claude-only-abilities.md). (1, the more fundamental one) `orchestrator org start <repo> <who>` - the step that starts the actual research work on the target member's own login - is hardcoded to a Claude session today: MindAttic.Orchestrator's OrgStartCommand never passes --provider, StartCommand.Settings.Provider defaults to "Claude", and its --account login path explicitly refuses any other provider ("--account is a Claude login: X has none", confirmed from Program.cs source). So there is no cross-CLI "start this under their own Codex/Kimi/agy" path at all yet, independent of messaging. (2) The final "tell the asker" step still depends on ListAgents/SendMessage/AskUserQuestion, Claude-only mechanisms with no confirmed Codex/Kimi/agy equivalent for reaching a specific, already-running peer conversation live. A generic ASYNC substitute for (2) already works with no new code: the ticket this ability files gets closed with the answers as a note when the work lands (step 4 below), and any CLI can already poll `tickets ticket show <ID> --json` for that - it just isn't an instant push.

**Confirmed finding, still not a bridge:** MAT-T98 checked the notify-back half specifically (it is not the same gap as /allocate's). The member this ability reaches runs on a DIFFERENT org member's own login - a different top-level CLI process, started separately via `orchestrator org start <repo> <who>`, not a child of this session. Codex's multi_agent_v2 spawn_agent family (the real equivalent found for /allocate) is explicitly the wrong mechanism here - MAT-T100 confirmed it only spawns a nested mid-turn child of the SAME session, architecturally distinct from Codex's separate top-level-session concept. That separate concept does exist and is real, non-experimental, no feature flag: `codex agents` (browse every session on the local app-server daemon), `$CODEX_HOME/session_index.jsonl` (the same list as a plain file), and `codex queue --thread <uuid|name> --message <text>` (push a message into an existing session from outside it) are all stable top-level `codex` subcommands today. But "the shared local app-server daemon" is scoped to one CODEX_HOME/one login - it does not reach a session running under a different org member's own login/account the way this ability needs. So it is a confirmed real primitive for same-login, cross-window messaging (a different, narrower feature nobody has asked for yet), not a bridge for this ability's actual cross-login need. Remains genuinely unbridgeable on Codex today for that reason, not just unverified - and MAT-T103 separately confirmed org start itself is Claude-only on every provider (see claude-only-reason), so this gap exists even before messaging comes into it. docs/claude-only-abilities.md has the full three-part breakdown.

## /schedule-wakeup

Generic, provider-agnostic "resume this CLI later without the user typing continue" mechanism (MAT-T103) - any CLI's own model can request its own scheduled resumption by running mindattic-agent-standard/schedule-wakeup.ps1, which re-invokes a chosen CLI's non-interactive mode in a given directory with a given prompt via a one-shot Windows scheduled task.

This is the portable equivalent of Claude Code's own `ScheduleWakeup` tool, built on Windows Task
Scheduler instead of a Claude-SDK-only primitive (MAT-T103, following up on MAT-T93/98's finding
that `ScheduleWakeup` had been written off as permanently Claude-only). Its real job - "re-invoke
this CLI non-interactively with a prompt at a future time" - needs nothing Claude-specific: every
CLI this workspace runs ships a non-interactive mode, and `schtasks` can fire any of them.

**Any CLI's own model may call this directly, proactively, the same way Claude calls its native
`ScheduleWakeup` tool** - this is not limited to a user-typed slash command. Reach for it whenever
you need to resume your own work later without anyone typing "continue": a pacing wait
(`shared/abilities/pacing.md`, `listen.md` step 3), a deferred follow-up, "check back on this in an
hour," or anything else that is "come back to this later" rather than "do it right now."

Run it as:

```
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File "mindattic-agent-standard\schedule-wakeup.ps1" `
  -Cli <claude|codex|kimi|agy> -WorkDir "<absolute working directory>" `
  -Prompt "<the resume instruction>" -DelayMinutes <n>     # or: -At "<absolute time>"
```

What it does:

1. **Computes a fire time** from `-DelaySeconds`/`-DelayMinutes` or an absolute `-At` time.
2. **Writes a small, self-contained wrapper script** (prompt text Base64-encoded, so quotes/newlines
   in it are never a problem) that: `cd`s to `-WorkDir`, invokes the chosen CLI's own confirmed
   non-interactive flag with the prompt, redirects all output to a UTF-8 log file (default: a
   `wakeup-logs` folder created as a *sibling* of `-WorkDir`, never inside a git-tracked repo),
   deletes its own scheduled task, then deletes itself - nothing lingers but the log.
3. **Registers that wrapper as a ONE-SHOT task** (`schtasks /create /sc once`).

Per-CLI non-interactive invocation, confirmed from each CLI's own `--help`/`exec --help` output
(MAT-T103, not guessed):

- `claude -p "<prompt>"` - cwd is read directly; no separate `-C`/`--cwd` flag.
- `codex exec -C "<dir>" "<prompt>"` - has an explicit working-root flag, passed alongside the cwd.
- `kimi -p "<prompt>"` - no `-C`/`--cwd` flag; relies on the wrapper's `cd` instead.
- `agy -p "<prompt>"` - no `-C`/`--cwd` flag; relies on the wrapper's `cd` instead.

Useful extras: `-ExtraCliArgs` passes through additional flags verbatim (nothing is added by
default - in particular this never silently adds a permission-bypass flag; decide that per call).
`-EnvOverrides 'KEY=VALUE'` sets process env vars before the CLI runs (e.g. pointing an isolated
test rig's `CODEX_HOME` at a scratch directory instead of a live one - the same safe-testing
convention MAT-T94/95/100 used). `-Cancel <TaskName>` deletes a scheduled wakeup that's no longer
needed. Full parameter docs are in the script's own comment-based help (`Get-Help
schedule-wakeup.ps1 -Full`).

**Tested end-to-end (MAT-T103, 2026-11-06)**: scheduled against `codex exec` with an isolated
scratch `CODEX_HOME` (the real, live one was never touched), fired on time, replied with the exact
requested text, logged it, deleted its own scheduled task, and deleted its own wrapper script -
confirmed by re-querying `schtasks` immediately before and after and seeing only the pre-existing,
unrelated scheduled tasks on this machine both times.

**Limitation**: the machine must be on and the triggering user's Windows session logged in at fire
time (this is a `schtasks` limitation, not something this script can route around) - fine for same
session pacing waits, not for "wake my laptop from being fully off."

## /test

Run the current repo's entire test suite, name every failure, and file a fix ticket for each. The one explicit way to ask for tests (agents never run them on their own, and /commit doesn't).

# /test - run a repo's whole test suite

Global MindAttic command (`/run tests` and `/run test` are aliases for it in Claude Code; see the
`tests` ability for the separate `/tests` alias command). This is the user explicitly asking for tests, so the "tests only when the
user says so" rule is satisfied for this one run. It runs the **whole** suite once, never a filtered
slice, and nothing re-runs it automatically afterwards.

## 1. Pick the repo and the revision

- The repo is `$ARGUMENTS` if given (a folder under the workspace root), else the repo the current
  directory is in. In the workspace root with no argument, ask which repo.
- Test what's on `origin/main`, not someone's half-done working tree: fetch, then use (or create) a
  clean detached worktree at `D:\Projects\MindAttic.worktrees\<Repo>\verify-main` checked out at
  `origin/main`. Never test in, reset or touch the main checkout.

## 2. Detect the suite

In the worktree, the first that applies:
- a `*.slnx` / `*.sln` at the root (or test projects under `tests/`): `dotnet test <solution> -nologo --logger "trx;LogFileName=tests.trx" --results-directory <out>`
- `package.json` with a `test` script: `npm test`
- `pyproject.toml` / `pytest.ini` / a `tests/` folder of `test_*.py`: `python -m pytest`
- `*.Tests.ps1` files: `Invoke-Pester -Output Detailed`
- `go.mod`: `go test ./...`
If none applies, say the repo has no test suite and stop.

## 3. Run it detached

A full suite can take 15+ minutes and the CLI may reap a background shell under memory pressure,
so start the run as its own process, with output to files in the scratchpad (`<out>`):

```powershell
$p = Start-Process <exe> -ArgumentList <args> -WorkingDirectory <worktree> -RedirectStandardOutput "<out>\stdout.txt" -RedirectStandardError "<out>\stderr.txt" -WindowStyle Hidden -PassThru
```

Then wait for that PID in a background shell command (`while (Get-Process -Id <pid> -EA SilentlyContinue) { Start-Sleep 20 }`)
and tell the user in one line that it's running, at which commit, and roughly how long it takes.
Don't poll; you're notified when the wait ends.

## 4. Report

- The totals line (passed / failed / skipped, duration) and the commit tested.
- Every failing test by name with its one-line error (from `stdout.txt` / the trx).
- All green: say so in one line and stop.

## 5. Failures become fix tickets

Group failures by likely cause and file one `--type fix` ticket per group in that repo
(`tickets ticket new --repo <Repo> --type fix --summary "<test(s)>: <symptom> (found by /tests)"`).
Fixes need no approval, so work them through subagents, one per ticket, all in the repo's own checkout on
`main` (the GOLDEN RULE: no separate branch or worktree, ever; subagents touch disjoint files):
find the root cause (product regression -> fix the code; stale or non-hermetic test -> fix the test, and
say why), verify with a **filtered** run of only its failing tests, commit with the ticket ID, land on
main and close the ticket. Never re-run the full suite on your own afterwards: when they've landed,
tell the user `/test` again will confirm it.

## /tests

Alias of /test - run the current repo's entire test suite, name every failure, and file a fix ticket for each.

# /tests - alias of /test

Read the `test` ability (in Claude Code: `~/.claude/commands/test.md`, source
`mindattic-agent-standard/shared/commands/test.md` under the MindAttic workspace root) and follow
it exactly, with `$ARGUMENTS` as its arguments. Don't keep a second copy of its steps here.

## /undock

Drop this CLI's own tab from the dashboard (or another's, by id) without ending the CLI — it keeps running headless; /dock (or the dashboard's own "Dock now") brings it back. /undock [SESSION].

Run `orchestrator undock $ARGUMENTS` (no arguments: this CLI's own session, from its `MINDATTIC_TERM_ID`). It asks any running MindAttic.Orchestrator dashboard to drop this session's tab - the opposite of /dock (M.ORCH-T1448). The CLI itself is untouched and keeps running; nothing about it changes except that the dashboard stops showing it until /dock (or the dashboard's own "Dock now") brings the tab back.

Report the command's own result line to the user, verbatim or near enough.

## /unstuck

Recover a Windows desktop that stopped responding to clicks - release stuck input, kill hung/runaway processes, restart a hung Explorer.

Read `D:\Projects\MindAttic\Unstuck\commands\unstuck.md` and follow its instructions exactly,
substituting `$ARGUMENTS` for its argument placeholder. The canonical body lives in the Unstuck
repo, versioned alongside the recovery script and the UnstuckTaskbar tray app that also invokes it;
this ability is only the provider-neutral pointer to it, so it is never duplicated here.

## /<member> (e.g. /amy, /ryan, /waffle ...)

Template ability backing the per-org-member commands (/amy, /erin, /honey, /jordan, /ohleo199, /pdftransferjr, /ryan, /ryandebraal, /shampoo1232, /waffle, and any alias generated for an active org member) - "/<member> research <what>" hands them a research task (see the research ability); "/<member> pair [repo]" splits a repo's open tickets between you both and starts each working their share; anything else is a message to that member's running CLI, or opens one on their login with it.

**Unavailable on Codex today** - Same two-part finding as the research ability's (read that one, and docs/claude-only-abilities.md, for the full reasoning) - MAT-T103 traced this past SendMessage/ListAgents to a more fundamental reason. The "research <what>" branch starts work via `orchestrator org start <repo> <who>`, which is hardcoded to a Claude session regardless of the target member's own configured CLI (MindAttic.Orchestrator's --account login path explicitly refuses any provider but Claude, confirmed from source) - so there is no cross-CLI "start this under their own login" path yet. The plain-message branch still depends on ListAgents (to discover this session's own name/other running sessions) and SendMessage (to deliver a reply to a named peer session) - both Claude-only mechanisms with no confirmed equivalent for reaching a specific, already-running peer conversation live. A generic async substitute exists for "research": the filed ticket closes with a note when the work lands, pollable by any CLI via `tickets ticket show <ID> --json` - no live push needed to eventually learn the answer.

**Confirmed finding, still not a bridge:** Same finding as the research ability's (read that one for the full reasoning) - Codex's real, stable, non-experimental `codex agents`/session_index.jsonl/`codex queue --thread --message` trio is architecturally the right shape for "list and message other sessions," but it is scoped to one CODEX_HOME/one login's shared local app-server daemon, and this ability's whole point is reaching a DIFFERENT org member's own separate login. Not a bridge for this gap; genuinely unbridgeable on Codex today, confirmed rather than assumed. MAT-T103 additionally confirmed `orchestrator org start` itself never reaches a non-Claude session on any provider, so the gap predates messaging entirely.
